creator: Money & Macro
title: Why Japan industrialized before China
full_text:
In 1868, Japan was so poor and weak that just like
other ancient civilizations like China and Egypt,
it was staring down the barrel of Western
colonization. Yet, where other industrialization
efforts crashed and burned, Japan's 19th century
industrialization remained the fastest economic
miracle in history till perhaps the rise of
China a century later. So, how did they do
it? And why was Japan the only non-European nation
to industrialize so early? The standard answer is
the so-called Meji Restoration, which was started
by Japanese samurai that were worried that Japan
would soon be carved up like China. You see, just
like British gunboats forced China to open up
trade on unequal terms, in 1854, American gunboats
had forced Japan to sign a couple of unequal
treaties with Western powers, which forced them
to cap import tariffs at just 5%. Fearing for the
very future of Japan, in 1871, Okubo Toshimichi did
something unthinkable for a traditional samurai.
He cut off his samurai topnot, put on a Victorian
three-piece suit, and together with a core group
of reformers, he overthrew the reigning shogun
and replaced him with Emperor Meii. The Meiji
government wanted a strong military. So in
the 19th century, that meant steel, warships,
guns, railroads. In other words, Japan needed
to industrialize fast. Enrich the country,
strengthen the military. That was the job of
Okubo Toshimichi. But that was easier said
than done. Egypt had famously tried and failed for
decades to industrialize. And even the mighty Qing
dynasty's 1961 selfstrengthening movement was
increasingly looking like a massive failure.
Yet in just 30 years time, Okubo's home ministry
had overseen the rise of a diversified industrial
base that allowed Japan to defeat a major European
power in open war, to end the unequal treaties,
and to rather than be colonized, to become the
colonizer instead. But why did Okubo succeed
where so many others failed? How did he not only
modernize Japan but create a playbook that would
later form the basis for the Korean, Taiwanese,
and Chinese economic miracles in the 20th century.
Entire academic careers have been devoted to this
very question, and it's very easy indeed to either
oversimplify it or to get lost in the details.
Yet, after months of research, I think that I've
boiled down the essence of the Meiji miracle
to just five foundational building blocks.
Block number one, the government foundation. Block
number two, the liberal free market revolution.
Block number three, the big government push. Block
number four, the monetary creation tightrope.
Block number five, the Meji secret sauce. And as
we will see on their own, these building blocks
are not enough. Only together can they explain why
Japan industrialized first. Okay, building block
number one is actually pretty uncontroversial.
But how far the Meiji government went in it, even
changing the Japanese language itself honestly
surprised me. It is building block number one,
the government foundation. To understand how this
worked, consider the life story of a young boy,
Sakichi Toyoda, born in 1867. Every night,
Sakichi fell asleep to the rhythmic, exhausting
clack clack clack of his mother laboring over
a primitive wooden handloom. His father was a
humble carpenter. Had he been born in old Japan
or across the sea in Qing, China, Sakichi's destiny
would have been set and kind of boring. He would
live and die a carpenter. He was expected to be
illiterate, poor, and quiet. Luckily, Okubo's Meiji
Revolution shattered those rules. But to be clear,
Okubo had a really good base to start from since
literacy rates in Japan were already higher than
in the mainland before the major restoration. Yet
the new government went into overdrive to push
them even higher. In 1872, the Maji government
introduced a modern westernstyled national
education system. Rural populations initially
found these schools actually unfamiliar and
alien. Yet, school attendance skyrocketed from
an estimated 45% in 1870 to over 98% by 1901. As
a consequence, national literacy surged past 90%
by 1910, producing a uniquely qualified workforce
foundation for Japan's upcoming industrialization.
But Okubo understood that basic literacy and
mastering complex technical engineering
are two very different things. Therefore,
with his home ministry, he created the industrial
promotion bureau to supercharge the imports and
translation of western technical textbooks. The
scale of this linguistic operation was actually
quite staggering. Recent research by economists
Huas Shakab and Weinstein show that in 1870,
technical books were exclusively available
in European languages like English, France,
and German. So it didn't matter if you could read,
you could not read these types of books. However,
by 1910, the landscape had completely transformed.
Japanese language technical literacy was trailing
only French and English, putting Japan on
a completely different level than any other
Asian nation. But their research reveals that
this wasn't just a matter of running a routine
translation office. The Maji government actually
had to alter the very fabric of the Japanese
language to accommodate the industrial revolution.
You see, when cuttingedge technologies were
invented in Britain, it of course led to a wave of
new words in the English language like railroad,
steam engine or telegraph. Translating these
concepts into related languages like French or
German was relatively easy. However, for Japan,
there was a massive risk that translators would
come up with hundreds of different translations
for, for example, the word telegraph. And
therefore, the Maji government massively expanded
earlier translation efforts using standardized
technical dictionaries that triggered an absolute
explosion of new words in the Japanese language
after the Maji government came to power. Now the
timing of this all could of course not have been
more perfect for Sakichi Toyota who even though he
was born poor had access to a state school where
he learned to read and thanks to this language
basis Toyota could of course read technical
magazines and he famously read Samuel Smiles
British self-help book which Toyota credited
with setting him on the path to becoming an
inventor. However, reading books is only half
the battle. To really supercharge knowledge
catch up to the west, Okubo's home ministry
subsidized Japanese students that wanted to study
abroad. And they also brought knowledge to Japan,
paying foreign advisers exorbitant salaries to
train locals. And they organized expositions
where government imported machines and then showed
these to entrepreneurs. And Toyota famously built
his first patented wooden loom only after visiting
the third national industry exposition in Tokyo,
a massive event organized by the Matei government
to explicitly showcase these machines to study by
people like Toyota. However, when Sakichi tried
to upgrade his famous wooden looms to steel,
he hit a wall. In 1905, his prototype steel looms
literally shook themselves to pieces as they were
utterly humiliated in endurance tests against
British looms from the legendary Plat Brothers.
Desperate, Sakichi took a massive risk. He hired
an American master machinist, Charles Francis,
to help him out. But to pay his exorbitant
salary, Sakichi actually had to pay a lot of
that out of his own wage. But while he lived on
the edge of ruin, sacrificing his own livelihood,
he did in fact end up learning the secrets of
precision steel engineering. But while technical
knowledge allowed Toyota to become an inventor, it
was Okubo's aggressive infrastructure investment
push that allowed him to become a truly scalable
business. Toyota could of course never have made
metal looms without government train lines to
transport them to clients across the country.
And he could not have coordinated a modern supply
chain without government constructed telegraph
lines. And his primary customers, the textile
mills, only operated because they could import
ra cotton and export finished goods through modern
state funed boards on state subsidized ships. So
while there were also many smart ambitious young
people like Sakichi in China or Korea, they simply
lacked the access to advanced technical
knowledge and physical infrastructure that
the Miji government handed to Toyota. Yet if the
state had just built infrastructure and education,
Sakiichi would actually still never have become
Japan's greatest inventor. Which brings us to
building block number two, the liberal free market
revolution. Building block two is exactly where
the Maji reforms differed radically from the
ChineseQing reforms. You see, theQing tried
to build Western industries with conservative
cultural Asian values. Yet, when Okubu Toshimichi
traveled the world in the early 1870s to study
western industry, he realized that Japan had to
import more than just machinery. To compete with
the west, Japan's centuries old, rigid, feudal
cast system had to be completely dismantled. This
social revolution had a massive, massive immediate
impact on the fortunes of ordinary citizens
like Sakichi Toyota. under the old Tokugawa
feudal structure. Sakiji as the son of a humble
carpenter was restricted by both rigid cast and
guilt systems from ever really truly scaling
a disruptive manufacturing company. Therefore,
abolishing the class system was the first crucial
step to unlock Japan's human potential. However,
simply being allowed to trade was not enough to
convince people to risk their life savings on
unproven technologies. Therefore, in 1885, the
Maji government passed the Patent Monopoly Act,
a legal shield that Toyota later explicitly
credited as the primary spark that motivated
him to become a professional inventor. Together,
building blocks one and two sound like a textbook
triumph of classical economic 101. The government
took care of infrastructure and education, got rid
of bad regulations, secure property rights, and
simply stepped back then to let the free market
work its magic. However, there is a massive
glaring problem with this simplistic handsoff
narrative, and that is Argentina. You see, at this
exact same time on the other side of the planet,
Argentina was undergoing its own jaw-dropping,
some would say, economic miracle. By exploiting
vast tracks of cheap land and flooding the market
with agricultural exports, Argentina became almost
as rich as Great Britain on paper. However,
despite looking like the rise of Japan at first,
Japan actually industrialized, which later allowed
Japan to truly join the rich world while Argentina
was left behind. This puzzling divergence is
what famously led the Nobel laurate economist
Simon Knet declare that there are four kinds of
countries in the world. Developed, underdeveloped,
Japan and Argentina. So why did 19th century
Japan successfully industrialized while 19th
century free marketloving Argentina failed at
industrialization. This brings us to building
block number three, the big push. You see in
development economics the big push theory was
first proposed by economist Paul Rosenstein Rodan
in 1943 and he stated that industries in poor
nations suffer from a coordination problem and
that to solve it a country must launch a massive
coordinated investment push across multiple
dependent industries all at once. To see this
in practice let's look at Sakichi's Toyota's steel
loom factory. To build these advanced steel looms,
Sakichi needed a steady supply of highquality
coal and iron. However, importing these heavy raw
materials from Europe was prohibitively expensive.
And therefore, Japan desperately needed its own
domestic mining industry. But who on earth would
risk a life savings opening a coal mine when there
were no modern factories to buy all of that
coal? Should Toyota wait to build a factory
until the mines existed? Or should the mines
only exist if Toyota's factories were already
running? The answer is simply that without some
intervention, neither of these would get built,
at least not quick enough. And this is why Akubo's
home affair department stepped in to play the role
of the ultimate grand coordinator under a national
policy called promoting production and encouraging
industry. They did not just write checks. They
actually built model factories like the Shinmachi
spinning mill to show private entrepreneurs how
modern manufacturing was supposedly done. And for
heavy industry, they went even further directly
constructing state-of-the-art installations like
the Nagasaki shipyard and the massive Miki
coal mine. Sakichi could only make advanced
steel looms because Okubo had given the textile
and mining industries that Sakichi depended on a
big push. However, as state planners all over
the world would discover in the 20th century
under communism, coordinating an entire national
economy by just a government is incredibly hard.
And indeed, Okubo's state-run enterprises quickly
became notorious money fits plagued by massive
operational inefficiencies. And to make matters
worse, Toshimichi faced a violent backlash at
home. In 1877, his former friend Saigo Takamorei
led the southern samurai in the Satsuma Rebellion,
arguing that modernization was just moving far
too fast in Japan. And although the government
eventually crushed the rebellion, the financial
cost was so massive that it forced the Maji
government to turn to the printing presses,
sending the Japanese economy into a spiral of
hyperinflation. And to make matters worse, while
his side would prevail, the Satsuma rebellion's
fallout would prematurely end Okubo's role in
the maji economic miracle. In 1878, while riding
his carriage, he was ambushed and assassinated by
conservative samurai men who felt betrayed by his
modern world. When they searched his body, they
then found that he was actually carrying a letter
from his old friend, third turd rebel rival, Saigo
Takamorei. Okubu had sacrificed his friendships,
his culture, and finally his life to build the
foundations of modern Japan. Yet he died nearly
broke, having poured even much of his personal
funds into now failing state enterprises. So with
the country on the brink of financial collapse,
the government turned to a man who could not
be more different. Okubu's former disciple,
Matsucata Masayoshi. Unlike his charismatic,
visionary mentor, Matsucata was a numbers driven,
quiet, gentle man. Yet, as it would turn out,
a quiet calculating numbers man was precisely what
Japan needed. You see, to kill hyperinflation,
Matsucata presented himself as a brutal fiscal
hawk. He slashed government spending, sucked
cash out of circulation and let interest rates
skyrocket. Millions of poor farmers went bankrupt,
and Matsucata became the most hated man in Japan.
However, a closer look by historian Steven J.
Ericson actually reveals Matsugatu didn't just
blindly cut budgets all across the board. Instead,
he targeted only the state's worst inefficiencies.
And therefore, Erikson called his policy
expansionary austerity, not full-blown austerity.
And perhaps even more importantly, Matsucata
realized that while the state-led big push had
succeeded in building the physical infrastructure,
the government was simply terrible at running
day-to-day businesses. and therefore he engineered
a brilliant pivot. Rather than liquidating these
failing state-owned enterprises, Matsucata sold
them off at a fire sale to wealthy, well-connected
merchant families. And these families bundled the
assets into highly diversified mega corporations
known as Zybatsu like Mishubi, Mitsui, and
Sumitomo. To sweeten the deal, the government even
granted these Zybatsu mega corporations, private
banking licenses, and lucrative monopolies over
state shipping routes and mines. But crucially,
this did not mean that the Mei state left industry
completely to the free market. No, they remained
heavily involved in high-risk infrastructure
projects and heavy industries like Yawata steel
works. And crucially, to avoid falling prey to
the type of crony capitalism that ruins almost
every developing country it touches, Matsucata let
the Zibatu compete amongst each other ruthlessly
to ensure efficiency. Just as importantly, these
lucrative monopolies on mines and transport routes
were strictly conditional on performance. If
a Zibbatu failed to run a mine productively,
then the state would simply take it away
and hand it to a competitor. Therefore,
as economists Randall Mor and Masau Nakamura
argue, the Zibbatsu were not a parasitic
oligarchy. They were simply a more efficient
solution to give Japanese industries the big
push that they needed to power Japan's shocking
military victories in the first SinoJapanese war
in 1895 and the Russo European power Japanese
war in 1905 which Japan won. And by defeating a
major European superpower like Russia, Japan had
really proved that it could no longer be treated
as a secondass nation which ended the unequal
treaties. And while he was not there to see it,
Okubo's original mission, enrich the
country, strengthen the military,
was now officially complete. However, 1905 was
not the end of the road for Sakei Toyota. In fact,
his ultimate success would rely directly on
this unique Zibatu system. You see, when China's
Boxer Rebellion broke out, Toyota's textile
exports to China crashed to practically zero,
threatening to bankrupt his young firm. And in a
pure free market, his company would have surely
died right then and there. However, because Toyota
had the deep pocketed Mitsui Zibbatsu backing him.
Well, he could tank the losses and restructure
Toyota's business. And this meant that in 1929,
he served the ultimate poetic justice to the
British Plat brothers, whose superior machines
embarrassed Toyota decades earlier. They admitted
defeat. They bought the patent rights to Toyota's
revolutionary type G automatic loom for £100,000.
The student had officially become the master,
but Sakichi was dying. On his deathbed in 1930,
he looked at his son Picho and he did not tell
him to keep building looms. Instead, it said that
he handed him the massive British payout and gave
him one final challenge. I did my part with
textiles. Now you use this money to build the
Japanese automobile. Ultimately it was roughly
around this time that Argentina truly stagnated
as an agrarian nation and also turned to more
state involvement looking at Japan trying to
industrialize. But it became clear that Japan had
provided the blueprint for the world when it comes
to a state and mega corporation guided big push.
So, this is where our story could end. But for me,
it was not enough. I still had two nagging
questions that standard economic theory, even with
the big push building block, struggles to answer.
Number one, how did a dirt poor country like Japan
actually pay for all of this without drowning in
foreign debt? And second, sure, Japan's government
had increased education and infrastructure, but
didn't established Western competitors enjoy these
advantages already? How did Japanese startups like
Toyota actually out compete established Western
giants who already had a decadesl long head
start? To answer these two nagging questions,
we have to look at our next building blocks.
Starting with building block number four,
dual monetary manipulation. Okay. To understand
how the initially poor Miji government financed
its economic miracle, we have to understand
the dual nature of money creation. First,
there is the type of money that the state cannot
create. Foreign money like British pounds, gold or
silver at the time. This was arguably the most
important type of money for an industrializing
state like Japan because it needed it to import
advanced western machinery and to hire very
expensive foreign technical experts. At the time,
standard economics prescribed that a developing
state should borrow foreign money, of course, to
industrialize. Then when the industrialization was
complete, the state could repay these loans thanks
to export revenues in gold, pounds, and silver.
However, the fate of Egypt served as Okubo's and
Matsucata's ultimate horror scenario. You see,
Egypt had borrowed to the hilt to fund a state-led
big push industrialization effort. However,
Egypt's ability to pay back those loans
depended entirely on exporting cotton.
And when the American Civil War ended and cheap
American cotton flooded back onto global markets,
Egyptian cotton prices crashed and Egypt could
no longer service its debts. Next, Western
powers used those unpaid debts as a convenient
pretext to militarily invade and colonize Egypt,
the exact fate the Maji samurai were trying to
prevent. So instead of borrowing, Okubo and later
Matakata tried their best to fund every single
foreign import using the cash generated from
domestic exports. However, this left a major
puzzle. How do you jumpstart domestic export
industries without foreign money from foreign
borrowing for these machines and knowledge?
This is where domestic money creation comes in.
In a sovereign government, they can essentially
print this out of thin air. This only becomes
inflationary if it's not backed by a corresponding
increase in real economic production. Therefore,
if you print money to build a productive factory,
you can theoretically increase both the
supply of money and the supply of goods,
keeping prices stable. However, it could take
years for factories to become operational. So,
to prevent inflation, Okubo turned to taxation.
Under the old feudal shogunut, taxes were paid in
physical rice. However, this meant that government
revenue fluctuated wildly depending on the weather
and crop yields, making long-term planning and
investment in factories impossible. Therefore,
Okubu introduced a radical 3% land tax based
strictly on the monetary value of the land to
be paid exclusively in cash. Not only did this
stabilized state revenue needed for the big push
by changing from rice to currency, it greatly
incentivized ordinary Japanese people to turn to
open bank accounts. And this allowed statebacked
banks and private Zibatu conglomerates to further
increase the money supply through private bank
credit creation to fund upcoming industries. But
to prevent unproductive use of credit, the state
and Zibatu banks had highly targeted productive
mandates. State banks lend money strictly
for agricultural development, for example,
while Zibatu banks funded mines, shipping lines,
and heavy manufacturing. This was not yet used
for stock market speculation or housing bubbles
like we may see today. And because nearly every
newly created yen went directly into expanding
productive capacity, the supply of goods roughly
kept pace with the supply of money, keeping
inflation firmly in check. However, this very
success did greatly threaten Japan's access to
foreign money. You see, the domestic money supply
grew and Japan's citizens got richer. Of course,
then they wanted to buy consumer goods. But
because Japan's own industries were still in their
infancy, Western factories could produce goods
far more efficiently and cheaply than Japanese
startups. Therefore, citizens naturally wanted
to use their new money to buy superior western
imports for which they needed pound, silver,
or gold. That the state and industry of course
needed to import machines and knowledge. That's
a problem. Therefore, historically, developing
nations like the United States tended to protect
their young infant industries from foreign
competition behind giant tariff walls, decreasing
imports. However, remember those unequal treaties
without the ability to raise tariffs. There was a
very real risk that Japan's advanced industries
would be strangled in their cradle by cheap
Western imports, regardless of how much capital
the state banks and zibatu poured into them. So,
how did Japan manage to protect its domestic
industries and conserve precious silver and gold
when it was legally forbidden to use tariffs? This
brings us to the final crucial ingredient of the
Maji miracle, the Magi secret sauce, which I think
you could summarize as stealthily suppressing
imports and secretly encouraging exports. So, how
did the Maji Samurai do this? Well, I think there
are four main strategies that we actually still
often see today. The first is export subsidies.
Under Okubu, this was pretty direct as he
gave, for example, just money to Japanese
shipping companies, helping exports. But also, the
seemingly orthodox Matsucatu started the practice
of subsidizing exports, supporting banks via the
newly created central bank. Even Masugatus's fire
sales of state factories to zibatus at absolute
bottom of the barrel prices. Well, you could look
at this and say, well, that's clearly a failure of
the state. They're giving away money for free. But
you could also say it was actually a masterclass
in d-risking. You see, by building these factories
first, the state essentially absorbed the risk
100%. So then when the Zabatu took them over,
they started on a much closer footing to western
conglomerates which had had factories for decades.
Second, Japan gave rising industries a massive
boost simply by only procuring Japanese companies
for state projects such as railroads or
navy ships. This massively predictable
state demand meant that affected Japanese heavy
industries essentially didn't have to worry about
foreign competition for years. Third, and perhaps
entirely by accident, Matsugatu premiered a staple
of Asian development miracles, undervaluing your
currency when he chose to keep Japan on the silver
standard when most of the Western world shifted
collectively towards the gold standard. You see,
because this massive global shift meant that the
value of silver collapsed to gold, it also meant
that the value of the yen, which remained tight
to silver automatically depreciated against the
US dollar and the British pound. And as a result,
Japanese products became much cheaper compared
to the West even though tariffs were low. This
simultaneously helped reduce imports and boosted
exports, making more international money available
for importing machines and knowledge. But perhaps
the darkest part of the Japanese development
miracle was that while it greatly improved
the life of poor, highly talented people like
Sakichi, Japanese industry was also built on a
dark foundational reality. The brutal exploitation
of the Japanese workforce. You see, while the
West introduced labor protection laws, Japanese
workers enjoyed none of these. Japanese factories
routinely ran grueling 14 to 16-hour shifts
and heavily exploited young female peasants,
contract laborers who were housed in restrictive
factory dormitories. Meanwhile, the Maji state
suppressed labor unions, outlawing strikes, and
viewed organized labor as a dangerous socialist
threat. Again, this benefited both exports
by allowing Japanese startups to consistently
undercut Western competition on price because
they had to pay lower wages. And simultaneously,
these low wages kept imports low, allowing the
Maji government to preserve its precious gold and
foreign reserves and completely avoid the Egyptian
debt trap. Yet, it was this very strategy that
arguably caused Japan to fall into its own trap
and become a fascist military dictatorship after
the Great Depression plunged large parts of the
already poor export oriented Japanese workforce
into poverty. It was under these conditions
that rogue elements of the Japanese army started
violently targeting Japan's wealthy elites like
the director general of the Mitsui Zibbatsu. As
the public supported the violence given their
terrible circumstances, this arguably set the
scene for the civilian government to completely
surrender eventually to the powerful military,
which later plunged Japan into World War II, which
of course ultimately destroyed its industries. But
that's the story for another time. For now, I hope
you found this insightful, this deep dive into the
story of Japanese legends like Okubu, Matsugatu,
and Sakichi Toyota. I hope it was insightful to
see how the Maji miracle can be explained by a
combination of standard free market economics,
sure, but also big government and zybatsuleled
pushes and a set of forbidden techniques,
many of which you can still clearly see today
in major inspired economic miracles like those
of Taiwan, Korea, and China. This was my modern
interpretation of this story. But what if you
had lived in the late 19th century and early
20th century when this all happened? Well,
in that case, you could read all about the events
of the Maji restoration and the rise of Japan if
you consistently read our advertising sponsor,
The Economist. And even today, if you don't want
to miss the next development miracle, I highly
recommend you check out their coverage on the
ascent of India's economy, Vietnam's fast but
fragile rise, and finally their analysis on
how East Asia should respond to the rapid rise
of Chinese industry. As these analysis show,
The Economist delivers insights that truly help
you to see the bigger picture. And this is why
I highly recommend that you subscribe to The

You'll always stay on top of the latest global

notes.context_paragraph: Fearing for the very future of Japan, in 1871, Okubo Toshimichi did something unthinkable for a traditional samurai. He cut off his samurai topnot, put on a Victorian three-piece suit, and together with a core group of reformers, he overthrew the reigning shogun and replaced him with Emperor Meii.

sources.explanation: This confirms that technical knowledge was concentrated in these languages, including Italian, and uses the qualifier "most" rather than "exclusively."

notes.note: The overthrow of the Tokugawa shogunate and restoration of Emperor Meiji occurred in 1868, not 1871. Ōkubo Toshimichi and other reformers ousted the last shogun, Tokugawa Yoshinobu, in a coup on January 3, 1868.
notes.claim: Okubo Toshimichi and a core group of reformers overthrew the reigning shogun and replaced him with Emperor Meiji.
notes.context_quote: together with a core group of reformers, he overthrew the reigning shogun and replaced him with Emperor Meii.
notes.context_paragraph: Fearing for the very future of Japan, in 1871, Okubo Toshimichi did something unthinkable for a traditional samurai. He cut off his samurai topnot, put on a Victorian three-piece suit, and together with a core group of reformers, he overthrew the reigning shogun and replaced him with Emperor Meii.

sources.quote: Meiji Restoration, in Japanese history, the political revolution in 1868 that brought about the final demise of the Tokugawa shogunate
sources.explanation: Confirms the Meiji Restoration and the end of the Tokugawa shogunate occurred in 1868.

sources.quote: The restoration event itself consisted of a coup d’état in the ancient imperial capital of Kyōto on January 3, 1868. The perpetrators announced the ouster of Tokugawa Yoshinobu (the last shogun)
sources.explanation: Confirms the coup ousting the last shogun took place on January 3, 1868.

sources.quote: political power in practice was exercised by a small group of reformist leaders... notably Chōshū... and Satsuma
sources.explanation: Identifies the core group of reformist leaders (including those from Ōkubo Toshimichi's Satsuma domain) who held power.

sources.quote: Meiji Restoration, in Japanese history, the political revolution in 1868 that brought about the final demise of the Tokugawa shogunate (military government)—thus ending the Edo (Tokugawa) period (1603–1867)—and, at least nominally, returned control of the country to direct imperial rule under Mutsuhito (the emperor Meiji).
sources.explanation: Directly supports that the restoration of Emperor Meiji and the fall of the shogunate occurred in 1868.

sources.quote: The restoration event itself consisted of a coup d’état in the ancient imperial capital of Kyōto on January 3, 1868. The perpetrators announced the ouster of Tokugawa Yoshinobu (the last shogun)
sources.explanation: Confirms the specific date and nature of the coup against the last shogun.

notes.note: Extraterritoriality, the key unequal treaty provision, was abolished in 1899—five years before the Russo-Japanese War (1904-05). Only tariff autonomy came later, in 1911, as the final step of a long revision process, not a direct result of the war.
notes.claim: Japan's defeat of Russia contributed to the ending of the unequal treaties imposed on Japan by Western powers.
notes.context_quote: by defeating a major European superpower like Russia, Japan had really proved that it could no longer be treated as a secondass nation which ended the unequal treaties.
notes.context_paragraph: And by defeating a major European superpower like Russia, Japan had really proved that it could no longer be treated as a secondass nation which ended the unequal treaties.

sources.quote: Meanwhile, with the revision of the extraterritoriality treaties in 1894 (Meiji 27), extraterritoriality was abolished in 1899.
sources.explanation: Supports the claim that extraterritoriality was abolished in 1899, five years prior to the Russo-Japanese War.

sources.quote: And tariff (customs) autonomy was achieved in 1911 (Meiji 44), the longstanding issue of treaty revision finally was fully resolved.
sources.explanation: Supports the claim that tariff autonomy was the final step achieved in 1911.

sources.quote: These treaties were re-negotiated with the individual countries in the 1890s and the new treaties came into effect in July-August 1899.
sources.explanation: Confirms that the renegotiation leading to the end of the original unequal treaties took effect in 1899.

sources.quote: While the question of jurisdiction under the treaties had been largely settled, the question of Japan's tariff autonomy remained unresolved.
sources.explanation: Confirms that legal jurisdiction (extraterritoriality) was settled before tariff autonomy.

sources.quote: Dr Ayako Hotta-Lister in the final paper gave an account of how the Japanese, in a mood of increased confidence after the Russo-Japanese war, ended the earlier treaties with a view to concluding the Anglo-Japanese Tariff Treaty of 1911.
sources.explanation: Supports the claim that tariff autonomy in 1911 was the final step of a process influenced by post-war confidence.
